li.p: Identify the eigenvalues, and their multiplicities, of an n\times n matrix whose characteristic polynomial is (2-\lambda)^3(-3-\lambda)^{10}(5-\lambda). What can you conclude about the dimensions of the eigenspaces? What is the shape of the matrix? Do you have enough information to guarantee that there is a basis of \real^n consisting of eigenvectors?

Find the eigenvalues of
\left[\begin{array}{rr} 0 \amp -1 \\ 4 \amp -4 \\ \end{array}\right] and state their multiplicities. Can you find a basis of \real^2 consisting of eigenvectors of this matrix?

Consider the matrix A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} -1 \amp 0 \amp 2 \\ -2 \amp -2 \amp -4 \\ 0 \amp 0 \amp -2 \\ \end{array}\right] whose characteristic equation is
(-2-\lambda)^2(-1-\lambda) = 0 .
Identify the eigenvalues and their multiplicities.
For each eigenvalue \lambda, find a basis of the eigenspace E_\lambda and state its dimension.
Is there a basis of \real^3 consisting of eigenvectors of A?

Now consider the matrix A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} -5 \amp -2 \amp -6 \\ -2 \amp -2 \amp -4 \\ 2 \amp 1 \amp 2 \\ \end{array}\right] whose characteristic equation is also
(-2-\lambda)^2(-1-\lambda) = 0 .
Identify the eigenvalues and their multiplicities.
For each eigenvalue \lambda, find a basis of the eigenspace E_\lambda and state its dimension.
Is there a basis of \real^3 consisting of eigenvectors of A?

Consider the matrix A = \left[\begin{array}{rrr} -5 \amp -2 \amp -6 \\ 4 \amp 1 \amp 8 \\ 2 \amp 1 \amp 2 \\ \end{array}\right] whose characteristic equation is
(-2-\lambda)(1-\lambda)(-1-\lambda) = 0 .
Identify the eigenvalues and their multiplicities.
For each eigenvalue \lambda, find a basis of the eigenspace E_\lambda and state its dimension.
Is there a basis of \real^3 consisting of eigenvectors of A?
The dimension of the matrix is 14\times14 since the degree of the characteristic polynomial is 14. We cannot guarantee that we can form a basis for \real^{14} consisting of eigenvectors, however.
There is one eigenvalue \lambda=-2 having multiplicity two. Because the eigenspace E_{-2} is one-dimensional, however, we cannot find a basis for \real^2 consisting of eigenvectors of A.

For the 3\times3 matrix A,
We have eigenvalues \lambda=-2 with multiplicity 2 and \lambda=-1 with multiplicity 1.
The eigenspace E_{-2} is two-dimensional with basis \left\{\threevec{-2}{0}{1},\threevec010\right\}. The eigenspace E_{-1} is one-dimensional with basis vector \threevec{-1}20.
We are able to form a basis for \real^3 consisting of eigenvectors of A.

For the 3\times3 matrix A,
We have eigenvalues \lambda=-2 with multiplicity 2 and \lambda=-1 with multiplicity 1.
The eigenspace E_{-2} is one-dimensional with basis vector \threevec{-2}01. The eigenspace E_{-1} is also one-dimensional with basis vector \threevec{-1}{2}{0}.
It is not possible to form a basis for \real^3 consisting of eigenvectors of A.

For this matrix,
There are three eigenvalues \lambda=-2, -1, and 1, each having multiplicity 1.
A basis vector for the eigenspace E_{-2} is \threevec{-2}01. A basis vector for the eigenspace E_{-1} is \threevec{1}{-2}0. A basis vector for the eigenspace E_{1} is \threevec{-2}{3}{1}.
We can form a basis for \real^3 consisting of eigenvectors of A.
